results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text: No. Phasing in does not cause a permanent to enter the battlefield; it simply changes the permanent's status from "phased out" to "phased in." The rules explicitly state that zone-change triggers (which include enters-the-battlefield abilities) don't trigger when a permanent phases in or out, and effects that check a permanent's history won't treat the phasing event as having caused it to leave or enter the battlefield.

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text: When a creature has both trample and deathtouch, assigning combat damage becomes very efficient. Deathtouch means any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature is lethal for excess damage calculations (rule 702.2c). Trample requires you to assign lethal damage to all blockers before assigning excess damage to the defending player or planeswalker (rule 702.19b). Because 1 damage from a deathtouch source is already lethal, you only need to assign 1 damage to each blocking creature. Any remaining damage can then trample over to the player or planeswalker being attacked. Rule 120.4a confirms that for deathtouch sources, any damage greater than 1 is excess damage when dealing damage to a creature, so exactly 1 damage is sufficient to satisfy the lethal requirement for trample.

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text: Yes. Storm is defined as a triggered ability that functions on the stack (rule 702.40a). When you cast a spell with storm, the triggered ability goes on the stack above that spell. As a triggered ability on the stack, it can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities (rule 113.9); it remains on the stack until it's countered, it resolves, or another effect removes it (rule 603.3). It cannot be countered by effects that only counter spells, because triggered abilities are not spells.

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text: No, you cannot. A card's color identity includes all colors of mana symbols in its mana cost and rules text. A hybrid mana symbol like {R/G} is both red and green (rule 107.4e), so a card with that symbol has a color identity containing both colors. Commander deck construction requires that every color in a card's color identity be present in the commander's color identity (rule 903.5c). If your commander has only one of those colors, the card's other color is not in the commander's identity, making the card illegal.

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to the untap step. During the untap step, no player receives priority ([502.4], [117.3a]). Since priority is never given, no player can cast spells or activate abilities. Any abilities that trigger during the untap step are held and will be put on the stack when a player would next receive priority, which is usually in the upkeep step ([503.1a]). The untap step is one of the steps where no priority is ever given ([500.3]).

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text: Yes, creatures remain attacking creatures during the end of combat step. An attacking creature remains an attacking creature until it's removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first (rule 508.1k and the Attacking Creature definition). The end of combat step is the final step of the combat phase (see [End of Combat Step]), and creatures are only removed from combat as the step ends (rule 511.3). Additionally, effects that last 'until end of combat' expire at the end of the combat phase, not at the start of the end of combat step (rule 511.2), so those effects keep creatures attacking throughout the step. Of course, a creature could be removed from combat earlier by an effect that specifically removes it (rule 506.4a), but absent such an effect, it's still attacking during the end of combat step.

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text: No, you do not cast lands. Lands are never spells and are never cast. Instead, you **play** a land as a special action that doesn't use the stack. This is true even for cards that are both a land and another card type (like artifact lands) — they can only be played as lands, not cast as spells. Lands have no mana cost, and playing them doesn't involve paying any costs.

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text: Yes, you can sacrifice an evoked creature before its evoke triggered ability resolves. The evoke ability creates a triggered ability that goes on the stack when the creature enters. You can respond to that trigger by activating an ability or casting a spell that sacrifices the creature. Once the trigger is on the stack, it exists independently of its source (rule 113.7a). When the evoke trigger resolves, it instructs you to sacrifice the creature, but if the creature is no longer on the battlefield, you can't sacrifice it, and the trigger does nothing (or as much as possible).

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text: Yes, losing all abilities includes keyword abilities. Keyword abilities are simply a shorthand way of writing common abilities (rule 702.1), and they are still abilities. An effect that removes abilities (rule 113.10) will remove all abilities, including keyword ones, because any game text that defines what a permanent can or can't do is an ability (rule 113.2a).

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: Yes, you can draw cards even if you're already at your maximum hand size. The maximum hand size only matters during your cleanup step: at that point, if you have more cards than your maximum hand size, you must discard down to that number. There is no rule that prevents you from drawing cards simply because your hand is already full.

results.question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
results.text: When a planeswalker has exactly 0 loyalty counters, its loyalty is 0 (rule 306.5c), and it is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action (rules 306.9, 704.5i). The provided rules do not explicitly address a planeswalker having less than 0 loyalty counters, so the outcome in that case is not covered by these rules. In practice, damage removes loyalty counters and you cannot have negative counters, but that principle is not stated in the given rules.

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text: No, non-creature artifacts do not die. The term "dies" is defined as "is put into a graveyard from the battlefield" and applies only to creatures and planeswalkers. A non-creature artifact put into a graveyard from the battlefield is simply moved to the graveyard; it hasn't "died."

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text:
When you are required to draw a card (e.g., during your draw step or from a spell) and your library has no cards, you attempt to draw but no card moves from your library to your hand. Then, the next time state-based actions are checked, you lose the game [121.4][704.5b]. This is true even if you are forced to draw more cards than remain—you draw nothing and then lose [104.3c].

However, if an effect would replace that card draw (such as "If you would draw a card, instead …"), that replacement effect is applied even though your library is empty, and you may not actually draw a card—potentially avoiding the loss [121.6a][614.11].

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
The combat phase has five steps, which proceed in order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat. The declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped if no creatures are declared as attackers or put onto the battlefield attacking. There are two combat damage steps if any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike [506.1].

As the defending player, you receive priority during each of these steps after the active player has passed priority. At the start of each step (except end of combat, which has no turn-based actions [511.1]), any turn-based actions are performed and triggered abilities go on the stack. Then the active player gets priority. Once the active player passes, you (the defending player) get priority [117.3a]. In a two-player game, the nonactive player is automatically the defending player [506.2]. In a multiplayer game using the Attack Multiple Players option, all opponents are defending players and receive priority in APNAP order after the active player [802.2]. In other multiplayer variants, the active player may choose a defending player as a turn-based action at the start of the beginning of combat step [507.1], and that player (along with any other defending players dictated by the variant) will get priority after the active player in each step.

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a mana ability. Mana abilities don't use the stack; they resolve immediately after being activated. This means they can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. This applies to both activated mana abilities (like tapping a land for mana) and triggered mana abilities (like an enchantment that adds mana when a land is tapped).

results.question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
results.text: The provided rules don't settle whether you can respond to a cost being paid. They describe how costs are paid as part of casting spells or activating abilities, but they don't include the rules about the stack, priority, or the fact that paying costs doesn't use the stack and doesn't allow responses. Without those rules, I can't give a definitive answer.

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text:
Layers are the system Magic uses to determine the order in which continuous effects modify an object's characteristics. The game starts with the object's printed values (or the values defined by the effect that created it for tokens/copies) and then applies all applicable continuous effects in a strict sequence of layers, from 1 to 7 [613.1]. The layers are:

- **Layer 1:** Effects that modify copiable values, including copy effects and "as . . . enters" abilities that set power/toughness [613.1a]. Within this layer, sublayer 1a applies copiable effects [613.2a].
- **Layer 2:** Control-changing effects (e.g., Act of Treason's "gain control" part) [613.6].
- **Layer 3:** Text-changing effects [613.1c].
- **Layer 4:** Type-changing effects (card type, subtype, supertype) [613.1d].
- **Layer 5:** Color-changing effects [613.1e].
- **Layer 6:** Ability-adding effects, keyword counters, ability-removing effects, and effects that say an object can't have an ability [613.1f].
- **Layer 7:** Power- and toughness-changing effects. This layer has sublayers: 7a applies characteristic-defining abilities that define power/toughness [613.4a]; 7b applies effects that set power/toughness to a specific value; 7c applies effects that modify power/toughness (e.g., +1/+1 counters, +N/+N boosts) [613.5].

Within each layer or sublayer, effects are normally applied in timestamp order, but dependency can override that order if one effect depends on another [613.8, 613.8a]. If an effect has parts that belong in different layers, each part is applied in its appropriate layer, and the effect continues to apply to the same set of objects even if the ability generating it is removed [613.6]. The entire process is automatic and instantaneous—any change to an object's characteristics is immediately reflected [613.5].

This layered system ensures that all continuous effects interact in a predictable way, regardless of the order they entered the battlefield or resolved.

results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text: The legend rule is a state-based action that prevents a player from controlling two or more legendary permanents with the exact same name. Whenever state-based actions are checked (right before a player would receive priority), if a single player controls multiple legendary permanents that share a name, that player must choose one of them to keep. All the others are put into their owners' graveyards. This is not a sacrifice or destruction effect; it simply moves them to the graveyard as a game rule. The rule applies to any permanent with the legendary supertype, including creatures, artifacts, enchantments, lands, and planeswalkers (since planeswalkers now have the legendary supertype instead of the old planeswalker uniqueness rule). The choice of which permanent to keep is made by the player who controls them, and the rest are put into the graveyard simultaneously.

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text: Your creature dies the next time state-based actions are checked after the lethal damage is marked on it. State-based actions are checked right before any player would receive priority (for example, after a spell or ability resolves, or after combat damage is dealt). The game sees that the total damage marked on the creature is greater than or equal to its toughness, and the creature is destroyed as a state-based action. This destruction doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to. The damage itself doesn't destroy the creature; the state-based action does.

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text: No, you cannot cast your commander from exile simply because it is your commander. The Commander rules provide a state-based action that allows you to put your commander into the command zone if it is in exile (or the graveyard) since the last time state-based actions were checked [704.6d, 903.9a]. This is a move to the command zone, not a cast. The only zone from which the rules explicitly allow you to cast your commander is the command zone, with an additional cost for each previous cast from that zone [903.8]. To cast your commander from exile, you would need a specific effect that allows you to cast spells from exile (such as a card like 'Eternal Scourge' or 'Karn, the Great Creator'), and no such permission is inherent to the commander designation.

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text:
During the cleanup step, the following happens in order:

1. **Discard to hand size**: If the active player has more cards in hand than their maximum hand size (usually seven), they discard cards until they have that many. This is a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack (implied by [703.4p], which references discarding as a prerequisite for the next actions).

2. **Simultaneous turn-based actions**: Immediately after any discarding, all damage marked on permanents is removed, and all "until end of turn" and "this turn" effects end. These happen at the same time and don't use the stack [514.2, 703.4p].

3. **Priority (normally none)**: Normally, no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated [514.3]. However, there is an exception: the game checks for state-based actions and waiting triggered abilities (including those that trigger "at the beginning of the next cleanup step"). If any are found, those state-based actions are performed, then those triggered abilities are put on the stack, and then the active player gets priority. Players may cast spells and activate abilities. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins [514.3a, 704.3]. If no state-based actions are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting, the step ends without any player receiving priority [704.3, 500.3].

results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text:
State-based actions are checked automatically by the game rules, not controlled by any player, and they don't use the stack. They are checked:

- **Whenever a player would get priority** (including during the cleanup step if any state-based actions or triggered abilities are waiting). This is the primary timing: before any player receives priority, the game performs all applicable state-based actions, then repeats until none are performed, then puts waiting triggered abilities on the stack, and repeats again until nothing further happens. Only then does the player get priority. [704.3, 117.5]
- **During the cleanup step**, if state-based actions need to be performed or triggered abilities are waiting, they are checked and performed, then the active player gets priority. If nothing happens, no player gets priority and the step ends. [514.3a]
- **When an effect ends the combat phase** (e.g., Mandate of Peace) or **ends the turn**, state-based actions are checked as part of that process, and no player gets priority during that check. [724.2c, 724.1c]
- **After turn-based actions** at the beginning of a step or phase, state-based actions are checked before triggered abilities are put on the stack and before players receive priority. [703.3]

In all cases, state-based actions are performed as a single event, and the check repeats if any were performed, ensuring the game state is cleaned up before players can act.

results.question: when can I concede a game?
results.text: A player can concede the game at any time. This is a special action that doesn't use the stack, and it causes that player to leave the game immediately and lose. Even if another player controls your turn (e.g., via Mindslaver), you may still concede at any time. In Two-Headed Giant, if a player concedes, their entire team leaves the game and loses.

results.question: how do I know who the active player is?
results.text: The active player is simply the player whose turn it is. Rule 102.1 defines the active player as "the player whose turn it is," with all other players being nonactive players. So at any point in the game, look at whose turn is currently taking place—that player is the active player. In games using the shared team turns option, the active team is the team whose turn it is (rule 805.4a), but the concept of an individual active player still follows the same principle: the player currently taking their turn.

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: When a player casts a spell, they must have priority. After the spell is cast, the player who cast it receives priority again. This applies regardless of whether that player is the active player or not. So if a non-active player casts a spell, that non-active player gets priority first afterward.

results.question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: When the active player casts a spell, they had priority to do so. According to rule 117.3c, the player who had priority when they cast a spell receives priority again immediately afterward. Therefore, the active player gets priority first after casting their own spell.

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text: Yes. After you cast a spell, if you had priority before casting it, you receive priority again (rule 601.2i). This means you can immediately cast another spell or activate an ability before any other player gets a chance to respond. The general rule 117.3c also confirms that a player who casts a spell receives priority afterward. This is commonly referred to as "holding priority."

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
results.text:
Lore counters are put on Sagas in two ways:

1. **As they enter the battlefield** – A Saga without read ahead enters with one lore counter (rule 714.3a). A Saga with read ahead enters with a number of lore counters chosen by its controller between one and its final chapter number (rules 714.3b, 702.155b). Both are replacement effects.

2. **At the start of your precombat main phase** – As a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack, you put a lore counter on each Saga you control that has one or more chapter abilities (rules 714.3c, 703.4f, 505.4). This happens immediately after that phase begins.

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text: A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by effects generated when some spells or abilities resolve, or when some replacement effects are applied, that does something later on rather than at that time. It contains “when,” “whenever,” or “at,” although that word won’t usually begin the ability. It triggers only after it has been created, even if the trigger event occurred just beforehand.

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes, non-permanent spells (instants and sorceries) can have abilities. Rule 113.6 states that abilities of an instant or sorcery spell usually function only while that object is on the stack. Rule 113.3a explains that any text on an instant or sorcery spell is a spell ability unless it's an activated, triggered, or static ability that fits the criteria in rule 113.6. Additionally, rule 405.4 says each spell has all the characteristics of the card associated with it, so any abilities printed on the card are present on the spell while it's on the stack.

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text: Yes, you can activate a mana ability while a spell with split second is on the stack. Split second only prevents casting other spells and activating non-mana abilities. The split second rules explicitly state that players may activate mana abilities and take special actions while such a spell is on the stack.

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text: Counterspell resolves first because it's on top of the stack. When it resolves, it counters Divination, removing Divination from the stack and putting it into your graveyard. Divination never resolves and none of its effects occur.

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text: You must assign at least 3 damage to Vampire Nighthawk before trampling over. Trample requires you to assign lethal damage to all blockers first, and lethal damage is defined as damage equal to a creature's toughness (here, 3, since Nighthawk is a 2/3). The deathtouch ability on the blocker doesn't change this requirement—rule 702.2c only makes 1 damage count as lethal when the *source* dealing the damage has deathtouch, and your Charging Rhino does not have deathtouch.

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text: Yes, Monastery Swiftspear's prowess triggers when you cast the noncreature spell during the resolution of Shardless Agent's cascade ability. However, triggered abilities that trigger during the resolution of a spell or ability aren't put onto the stack until that spell or ability finishes resolving. So the prowess trigger waits until cascade has completely resolved, then goes on the stack above the cascaded spell. Because prowess resolves before the spell that caused it (as stated in its ruling), Monastery Swiftspear gets +1/+1 before the cascaded spell resolves.

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text: Yes. The Grizzly Bears already has 2 damage marked on it, which equals its toughness of 2. That means it has been dealt lethal damage. State-based actions are checked right before any player would receive priority—including after you cast Lightning Bolt but before it resolves. When that check happens, the game sees a creature with toughness greater than 0, damage marked on it, and total damage greater than or equal to its toughness, so the Bears is destroyed as a state-based action. It will be put into the graveyard before Lightning Bolt ever resolves.

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text: Both triggers go on the stack at the beginning of your upkeep. Yours goes on first, then your opponent's, so your opponent's resolves first. You don't get to choose the order between them.

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text: Only the original sorcery card returns to your hand. The copy created by Fork is a spell on the stack but has no physical card associated with it. Buyback's replacement effect ("put this spell into its owner's hand instead of into that player's graveyard as it resolves") applies to the original spell because you paid its buyback cost. The copy inherits the decision that buyback was paid, but since it isn't a card, there is nothing to put into your hand. As Fork ruling #8 states, "If you copy a spell for which Buyback has been paid, you get nothing back since the copied spell does not have a card to give you." The copy simply ceases to exist after it resolves (rule 704.5e).

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No, you do not get a token. The Mimic Vat ruling explicitly states that if the exiled card is a nonpermanent card (like an instant or sorcery) that was manifested, you can't create a token that's a copy of it, so no token is created.

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text: Yes, both exiled creatures return. Fiend Hunter has two linked abilities: the enters-the-battlefield ability that exiles a creature, and the leaves-the-battlefield ability that returns “the exiled card.” When you copy the enters-the-battlefield ability with Lithoform Engine, the copy is also linked to that same leaves-the-battlefield ability. As a result, “the exiled card” refers to all cards exiled by both the original ability and the copy. When Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield, its second ability triggers and returns both creatures to the battlefield under their owners’ control.

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text: No, the exiled creature does not return to the battlefield. Banishing Light's exile effect is a one-shot effect that returns the exiled permanent when Banishing Light leaves the battlefield. Phasing out does **not** cause a permanent to leave the battlefield (rule 702.26d), so the condition for the return effect is not met. As stated in Teferi's Protection's rulings, any one-shot effects waiting for "until [this] leaves the battlefield" won't happen when a permanent phases out. The creature remains exiled.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text:
Yes, your opponent can target Emrakul with Counterspell while it's on the stack. Protection from instants only functions while Emrakul is on the battlefield (see Emrakul ruling #2). On the stack, Emrakul is a spell and does not have that protection, so it's a legal target.

If Counterspell resolves and counters Emrakul, the spell is removed from the stack and goes to the graveyard. However, the triggered ability "When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent..." is a separate object on the stack that triggered when you cast Emrakul (rule 603.1a). It exists independently of the spell and will still resolve, even if Emrakul is countered. So you will still control that opponent's next turn and they will take an extra turn afterward.

Your opponent cast Counterspell in response to the cast trigger, which is allowed because players can cast instants while other spells/abilities are on the stack (rule 117.7). The trigger is above Emrakul on the stack, so Counterspell will resolve before the trigger, but that doesn't affect the trigger's existence.

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text:
Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a modal double-faced card. While it's in your library, it has only the characteristics of its front face (Valki), so its mana value is 2. Cascade exiles cards until it hits a nonland card with mana value less than the cascade spell's mana value. Since Valki's mana value is 2, it's a legal hit as long as the cascade spell's mana value is 3 or greater.

When cascade lets you cast the exiled card, you may cast either face of a modal double-faced card that fits the criteria. The cascade ability then checks whether the resulting spell's mana value is less than the cascade spell's mana value. Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor has mana value 7. Therefore, you can cast Tibalt for free only if the cascade spell's mana value is 8 or more. If the cascade spell's mana value is 7 or less, you cannot cast Tibalt (but you can still cast Valki, whose mana value is 2).
citations: [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16]

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
You control **one** of your opponent’s turns (the next one), and they will take **two extra turns** after that turn. You **do** get a second Emrakul — a token copy — but copying the Emrakul spell **does not** give you another control-a-turn trigger.

Here’s why:

1. **Copying the cast trigger**  
   Lithoform Engine’s first ability copies the triggered ability “When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player’s next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn.” The copy is put onto the stack and resolves just like the original (rule 707.10). Both the original and the copy will set up a control effect and an extra turn.

   According to Emrakul’s ruling #14, multiple player‑controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other — the last one to be created is the one that works. However, **each** ability’s effect still creates an extra turn. So if both the original and the copy target the same opponent, the one that resolves last will control that opponent’s next turn, and the opponent will take two extra turns after that turn (one from each resolution).

2. **Copying the Emrakul spell**  
   Lithoform Engine’s third ability copies the Emrakul permanent spell on the stack. A copy of a spell is **not cast** (rule 707.10b; Lithoform Engine ruling #6 confirms this). Because the copy isn’t cast, Emrakul’s “When you cast this spell” ability does **not** trigger — you get no additional control‑a‑turn trigger from the copy.

   The copy of a permanent spell becomes a token as it resolves (rule 111.13). That token has all the characteristics of Emrakul, the Promised End (a 13/13 legendary Eldrazi with flying, trample, protection from instants). So you do get a second Emrakul on the battlefield, albeit as a token. (The legend rule, which is not covered by the provided rules, would normally force you to put one into your graveyard, but the token itself is created.)

**Summary of the outcomes:**
- Opponent’s turns you control: **1** (the next turn).
- Extra turns the opponent takes: **2** (after that turn).
- Second Emrakul: **Yes**, a token copy.
- Additional control trigger from copying the spell: **No**.

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text: Yes, you get two tokens. When you copy Mimic Vat's activated ability with Lithoform Engine, the copy is put onto the stack and will resolve separately. The copy's source is the same Mimic Vat (Lithoform Engine ruling #0), so the phrase "this artifact" on the copy still refers to that specific Mimic Vat (rule 201.5a). When the copy resolves, it looks at the card currently exiled with that Mimic Vat and creates a token that's a copy of it, just as the original ability does (Mimic Vat ruling #4). Since the original ability hasn't resolved yet, the exiled card is still there, and both the original and the copy will each create a token. The copy of the ability has the same source as the original, so it functions identically (rule 707.10b).

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0, the mana cost is {G}{G}. Your cost reduction of {1} is generic mana, and rule 118.7a says generic reductions affect only the generic component of a cost. Since {G}{G} has no generic component, the reduction does nothing, leaving the cost at {G}{G}. Then Trinisphere's effect applies (Trinisphere ruling #0): because the mana component of the cost is only two mana, Trinisphere forces it to cost three mana. You would pay {3} (three generic mana) and create zero tokens.

For the best value, you should choose X=2. The mana cost becomes {2}{G}{G}. After applying the {1} generic reduction, the cost is {1}{G}{G} (three mana total). Trinisphere sees a cost of three mana and does nothing. You pay {1}{G}{G} and create two 1/1 tokens. This is the most tokens you can get while still paying only three mana under Trinisphere.

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text: Yes, you can cast Animate Dead targeting Grist, the Hunger Tide while it's in your graveyard. Because of Grist's first ability, it's a creature card in the graveyard, so it's a legal target for Animate Dead's "enchant creature card in a graveyard." When Animate Dead's enters-the-battlefield trigger resolves, it returns Grist to the battlefield. However, once on the battlefield, Grist is no longer a creature—it's just a planeswalker. Animate Dead's new enchant ability ("enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura") can't legally attach to a noncreature planeswalker. As a state-based action, Animate Dead is put into its owner's graveyard. This causes its delayed triggered ability ("When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it") to trigger. When that trigger resolves, you sacrifice Grist. The net result is that both Grist and Animate Dead end up in your graveyard.

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Yes, Skullbriar keeps the four +1/+1 counters. Its ability says counters remain on it as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library. When it dies, you may apply the commander replacement effect (rule 903.9b) to put it into the command zone instead of the graveyard. The command zone is not a hand or library, so the counters stay on Skullbriar there (as confirmed by ruling #3). When you recast it, it moves from the command zone to the stack and then to the battlefield — all zones where counters remain — so it enters the battlefield with those four counters still on it.

Doubling Season does **not** double those counters. Its replacement effect only applies when an effect would put counters on a permanent you control. The counters on Skullbriar are not being put on by an effect; they are simply retained due to its own ability. Skullbriar's ruling #2 explicitly states that effects like Doubling Season won't affect counters that remain on it as it changes zones.

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text: No, you do not lose the game during that extra turn. When you activate Sundial of the Infinite before the end step, the turn ends immediately and the end step is skipped entirely. Because the end step never occurs, the delayed triggered ability from Final Fortune (“At the beginning of that turn’s end step, you lose the game”) never triggers. However, according to Sundial’s ruling, any “at the beginning of the end step” abilities that are skipped this way will trigger at the beginning of the next turn’s end step instead. So you will lose the game at the beginning of the next turn’s end step unless you prevent that trigger as well.

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text: You choose what Clone copies as it enters the battlefield, not when you cast it. Clone's ability is a replacement effect that modifies how it enters (rule 616.1c). When the Clone spell resolves, it would normally enter as a 0/0 creature, but you apply the replacement effect instead. At that moment, you choose a creature already on the battlefield to copy, or choose to copy nothing (Clone rulings #2, #5). This choice doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to. Your opponent can, however, respond to the Clone spell while it's on the stack, before it resolves. Once Clone enters, the choice is already made and the opponent can't interact with that decision. The choice is not a target (Clone ruling #0), so hexproof or shroud don't prevent copying. The chosen creature's "as enters" choices are not copied; you make any such choices for Clone as it enters (rule 707.6).

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text:
You get three lands total: one from the original Flooded Strand ability and two from the copies created by Gogo, Master of Mimicry.

Here’s why:
- Flooded Strand’s ability is an activated ability that goes on the stack. Its cost (tapping, paying 1 life, and sacrificing the land) is paid only once, when you activate it.
- Gogo’s ability with X=2 copies that ability twice. According to rule 707.10b, a copy of an ability copies all decisions made for the original (modes, targets, etc.) but does **not** require paying costs again. The copies are put onto the stack and will resolve separately.
- Each copy (and the original) instructs you to “Search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle.” Because each ability is a separate effect that includes its own shuffle instruction, they resolve one after the other: you search, find a land, put it onto the battlefield, shuffle, then repeat for the next ability. Rule 701.23h (which merges multiple searches before a shuffle) does **not** apply here because each ability has its own shuffle step.
- Gogo’s ruling #6 confirms that the ability creates additional instances of the targeted ability on the stack, and ruling #8 confirms it can copy abilities without targets.

So you’ll end up with three lands from that one Flooded Strand activation.
